Best Session Replay Tools in 2026: 10 Platforms Compared (And the "Why" None of Them Capture)
Microsoft Clarity, FullStory, LogRocket, Hotjar and 6 more session replay tools compared on pricing, replay quality, and privacy risk — plus the one question no recording can answer.
Koji Research Team
AI Customer Research · July 29, 2026 · 11 min read
TL;DR: The best session replay tools in 2026 are Microsoft Clarity (free, unlimited, best starting point), FullStory (best enterprise replay quality and autocapture), LogRocket (best for engineering teams who need console logs and stack traces), Hotjar (best for CRO and UX teams), and PostHog (best if you want replay bundled with product analytics).
But every tool on this list answers the same question — what the user did.
None of them answer why .
That is the gap Koji fills: AI-moderated voice interviews that ask the customer directly, at scale, in hours.
What session replay actually is
Session replay software reconstructs a user's visit to your site or app. It is not literally video — most tools capture DOM mutations, mouse coordinates, scroll depth, clicks, and network events, then replay them as a synthetic video. That distinction matters for both performance and privacy, and we will come back to it.
Modern replay tools bundle three things:
Recordings — the replayable session itself.
Heatmaps — aggregated click, scroll, and attention maps.
Frustration signals — rage clicks, dead clicks, error clicks, and thrash detection.
Adoption is now mainstream rather than experimental.
Industry analyses put session replay in use at roughly 72% of enterprises as of 2024, and 71% of Fortune 500 companies had at least one session replay solution deployed across digital channels as of 2023.
Market sizing estimates vary widely by source, but the commonly cited figure for the dedicated session replay software category sits at roughly $323 million in 2026 , growing at a low-to-mid-teens CAGR.
In short: this is a solved, commoditized category. Which is exactly why the interesting question is no longer "which replay tool" but "what do I do once I have watched the recording."
The 10 best session replay tools in 2026
Pricing below reflects publicly listed rates at the time of writing and changes often — always confirm with the vendor, and see our user research tool pricing breakdown for how these fit a wider research budget.
1. Microsoft Clarity — best free option
Free, genuinely unlimited sessions, with heatmaps and AI-generated insights included.
There is no session cap and no paid tier to graduate into.
The trade-offs are shallower segmentation, weaker integrations, and the fact that your behavioral data lives in Microsoft's ecosystem.
For a team validating whether replay is useful at all, there is no reason to start anywhere else.
2. FullStory — best enterprise replay quality
Autocapture means you do not have to instrument events ahead of time; you can ask retroactive questions of data you did not know you needed. Rage-click and frustration detection are strong, and funnels and pathing are built in. Pricing is opaque and lands around $199/month for ~30,000 sessions , with enterprise agreements commonly $10,000+/year .
3. LogRocket — best for engineering teams
LogRocket pairs replay with console logs, network requests, Redux state, and stack traces.
When a bug report says "it broke," an engineer can watch the session and read the exception.
Entry pricing is around $69/month for 10,000 sessions .
Vendors in this space cite roughly 45% reductions in bug resolution time — plausible for teams whose bottleneck is reproduction, less so for teams whose bottleneck is prioritization.
4. Hotjar — best for CRO and UX teams
The gentlest learning curve in the category, with a free tier and paid plans from roughly $32–39/month .
Hotjar bundles recordings, heatmaps, and on-site surveys.
It is deliberately not an analytics platform, which is a feature for marketers and a limitation for data teams.
See our FullStory vs Hotjar comparison and Sprig vs Hotjar for head-to-heads.
5. PostHog — best bundled with product analytics
Replay is included alongside product analytics, feature flags, and experiments, with a usable free tier. If you are already on PostHog, adding a separate replay vendor is hard to justify. Our Koji vs PostHog comparison covers where it stops.
6. Contentsquare — best for enterprise digital experience
Zone-based analytics and revenue attribution per element, aimed at large ecommerce and financial services teams. Enterprise pricing, enterprise onboarding. See Koji vs Contentsquare .
7. Quantum Metric — best for quantified friction
Strong at attaching dollar values to friction points and surfacing anomalies automatically. Popular in retail and travel. Enterprise-only pricing.
8. Mouseflow — best budget paid option
See also: 9 best Mouseflow alternatives in 2026 . From roughly $31/month , with friction scoring and form analytics. A solid mid-market pick when Clarity is too limited and FullStory is too expensive.
9. Smartlook — best for mobile app replay
Update for 2026: Smartlook is now end of sale and can no longer be bought or renewed, and the platform is scheduled for decommissioning.
See 8 best Smartlook alternatives in 2026 for the dates and the data export deadline.
One of the stronger native mobile SDKs in the category, covering iOS, Android, and React Native — a real gap in several competitors.
10. Glassbox — best for regulated industries
See also: 8 best Glassbox alternatives in 2026 . Built around compliance and audit requirements, with heavy masking controls. Common in banking and insurance, where the privacy exposure below is a board-level concern.
The privacy problem nobody puts on the pricing page
Session replay carries legal exposure that most buyer's guides ignore.
Plaintiffs have argued that recording a visitor's interactions constitutes unlawful interception under state wiretapping statutes — most aggressively the California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA).
In Javier v.
Assurance IQ (Ninth Circuit, 2022), the court held that replay software recording activity before a privacy policy was presented violated consent requirements.
The filing volume is the real story. Annual CIPA filings went from 54 in 2022 to roughly 675 in 2024 , and consumer data privacy litigation is projected to exceed 3,500 filings in 2026 , with pixels and AI profiling the most-targeted practices.
Courts have split. Some have dismissed CIPA claims on the reasoning that replay data is reassembled after transmission and therefore is not intercepted "in transit." Others have let claims proceed. Consent — real consent, captured before recording starts — remains the most reliable defense.
The practical implication: session replay is data you collect about people who never agreed to be studied. An interview is data you collect from people who did. If your data residency and consent posture matters, read where your interview data actually lives .

Voice interviews, structured questions and automatic synthesis, in one workflow.
Start a free study
What every tool on this list cannot do
Watch a hundred recordings of users abandoning your checkout. You will see exactly where they stop. You will build a confident theory about why — and it will be a theory you invented, not one the customer told you.
Session replay is a behavioral instrument. It captures actions with perfect fidelity and intent with zero fidelity. A user who hesitates for eleven seconds on your pricing page might be doing mental math, might be checking a competitor tab, might be waiting for a colleague to reply on Slack. The replay looks identical in all three cases.
This is the same structural limit that applies to product analytics generally — we cover it in Product Analytics vs. User Research and A/B Testing vs. User Research . Quantitative behavioral tools are excellent at finding where the problem is and constitutionally incapable of explaining why it exists.
The traditional fix was to run follow-up interviews: recruit ten users, schedule them across two weeks, moderate each session yourself, transcribe, code the transcripts, and write it up. Six weeks later you have an answer to a question that mattered six weeks ago.
How Koji closes the loop
Koji is an AI-native customer research platform built for exactly this handoff. When your replay tool flags a drop-off, Koji interviews the people who dropped off.
AI-moderated voice interviews run at any hour, in parallel, with no scheduling and no moderator. Fifty interviews can run overnight instead of across three weeks.
Automatic thematic analysis clusters what customers said into themes with supporting quotes — no manual transcript coding.
Structured questions alongside open conversation. Koji supports six question types — open_ended , scale , single_choice , multiple_choice , ranking , and yes_no — so a single study produces both a satisfaction distribution and the verbatim reasoning behind it. Most research tools force you to choose between a survey and an interview.
Customizable AI consultants carry your product context, so the interviewer probes like someone who knows your business.
One-click reports turn a completed study into a shareable readout.
No moderator bias. The AI asks every participant the same core questions and follows up consistently, removing the interviewer effects that distort small-sample qualitative work.
Recruitment built in.
Reach the users who dropped off with personalised links from your own list when you want to track who answered, or a generic anonymous link when candour matters.
When you need people you do not have, describe the audience and Koji recruits them: approve a per-respondent quote in credits, and those interviews land in the same study.
The pairing is the point. Your session replay tool tells you that 34% of users abandon at the shipping step. Koji tells you that they abandon because the delivery estimate appears after the address form, and they assumed the date was unavailable. One is a metric. The other is a fix.
You can wire this together directly — see Google Analytics + Koji and Amplitude + Koji for triggering interviews from behavioral events, and Customer Journey Analytics for combining both data types.

If what you actually need is to know what threw rather than what the user clicked, the error-monitoring category is cheaper and more focused: see 9 best Sentry alternatives in 2026 .
For replay priced per 1,000 sessions on top of a two-part meter, see 8 best Datadog RUM alternatives in 2026 .
And at the enterprise end of the category, where neither the price nor the session cap is published at all, see 8 best Quantum Metric alternatives in 2026 .
How to choose
Budget of zero, want to learn the category: Microsoft Clarity.
Engineering-led debugging: LogRocket or Sentry Replay.
CRO and UX experimentation: Hotjar or Mouseflow.
Enterprise digital experience: FullStory, Contentsquare, or Quantum Metric.
Already on a product analytics platform: use its bundled replay before buying a point solution.
Regulated industry: Glassbox, with legal review of your consent flow.
Need the why, not just the where: Koji, which also finds the people for you when the users who dropped off are not on your list, and shows the price per completed interview in credits before you launch.
And whichever you pick, budget for the second half of the job. Recording behavior is cheap and increasingly free. Understanding it is where the value is.

Koji turns the questions your session replay tool raises into answers your customers give you directly — from question to insight in hours, not weeks, with no research expertise required. Teams replace six-week interview cycles with overnight studies and get 10x faster insights without hiring a researcher.
